steps.body: Every outcome either is in A or is not. So P(A) + P(not A) = 1, giving the **complement rule**: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). This is the workhorse for "at least one", because the opposite of *at least one* is the much smaller, much easier event: **none**.
Flip three coins. Eight equally likely outcomes.

widget.prompt: The 8 cells are the 8 outcomes of flipping three coins (HHH, HHT, … TTT). Shade the cells with at least one head, so the shaded fraction equals 7/8.
widget.successFeedback: Seven of eight. Only TTT has no head, so "at least one head" is everything else: 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.
widget.lowFeedback: Still short. Count backwards instead: exactly one outcome (TTT) has no head at all, so seven do.
widget.highFeedback: You cannot shade more than seven — TTT genuinely has no heads, so it must stay unshaded.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 7/8 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 4/8 here — and 7 is more. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: "At least one head" fails only when **every** coin is a tail. So its complement is "no heads at all" = TTT.
Complement means *everything else*. Everything else than "one or more heads" is "zero heads".

widget.prompt: Three coins are flipped. What is the complement of "at least one head"?

options.label: No heads at all (TTT)
options.feedback: Right — the only way to miss "one or more heads" is to get zero of them.

options.label: At least one tail
options.feedback: That is not an opposite: HHT has at least one head *and* at least one tail, so both events happen together. Complements can never overlap.

options.label: Exactly one head
options.feedback: Exactly one head is *inside* "at least one head", not opposite to it. The complement must contain none of A's outcomes.

options.label: All heads (HHH)
options.feedback: HHH is the most extreme case of "at least one head", so it belongs to the event itself, not to its complement.

explanationVariants: Count the misses: 5 × 5 = 25 outcomes show no 6. So 36 − 25 = 11 show at least one 6.
Direct count: six outcomes where the first die is 6, six where the second is 6, minus (6,6) counted twice → 11.

widget.prompt: Roll two dice. How many of the 36 outcomes show **at least one 6**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is 6 + 6. The outcome (6, 6) appears in both lists, so a plain sum counts it twice — subtract it once.
That is only (6, 6). "At least one" also includes rolls like (6, 2) and (3, 6) where a single die shows the 6.
That is the count of rolls with **no** 6. It is the complement — the answer is 36 − 25.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count what fails: 5 × 5 = 25 rolls have no 6, so 36 − 25 = 11 rolls have at least one.

steps.body: Notice the pattern. Counting "at least one" directly means adding overlapping cases and repairing double-counts. Counting **none** is one clean multiplication — every trial must miss. That is why the complement route is almost always the short road.

explanationVariants: Four coins give 2⁴ = 16 outcomes. Exactly one of them (TTTT) has no head, so 16 − 1 = 15 have at least one.
P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 1/16 = 15/16, i.e. 15 of the 16 outcomes.

widget.prompt: Flip four coins. How many of the 16 outcomes show **at least one head**?

commonErrors.feedback: That counts only the outcomes with **exactly** one head. "At least one" also allows two, three or four heads.
That is every outcome, but TTTT has no head at all, so it must be excluded — 16 − 1 = 15.
That is half of 16, the count for a single fixed coin landing heads. The event allows *any* of the four coins to be the head.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only TTTT fails, so 16 − 1 = 15 outcomes contain at least one head.

steps.body: Three dice — the direct count would be miserable.
hints: Do not count sixes. Count the rolls with **no** six.
Each die has 5 non-six faces, so 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 rolls miss entirely — out of 6³ = 216.
explanationVariants: P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)³ = 1 − 125/216 = 91/216, so 91 of the 216 rolls qualify.
216 total rolls, 125 with no six at all; every other roll shows a six somewhere: 216 − 125 = 91.

widget.prompt: Roll three dice (216 equally likely outcomes). How many show **at least one 6**?

commonErrors.feedback: That is the count of rolls with **no** 6 — the complement. Subtract it from 216 to get the rolls that do contain a six.
That is 216 × 1/2, which is what you get by adding 1/6 three times. Probabilities of overlapping events cannot simply be added.
That is 6 × 6, the count for one fixed die showing a 6. The other two dice still have to be accounted for.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the misses: 5³ = 125 rolls have no six, so 216 − 125 = 91 rolls have at least one.

steps.body: When the event is sprawling, count its opposite.
takeaways: P(not A) = 1 − P(A) — the complement rule.
The complement of "at least one" is "none", which is a single clean multiplication.
"At least one tail" is **not** the opposite of "at least one head" — complements can never overlap.
steps.teaser: Next: two events that cannot happen together — and why that is a special case, not the normal one.

concept.body: "At least one" means **one or more** — one, two, all of them. It fails in exactly one way: **zero**. So always ask "how many outcomes have zero?" and subtract that from the total.

explanationVariants: Two coins have 4 outcomes; only TT has zero heads, so 4 − 1 = 3 have at least one head.
P(at least one head) = 1 − P(TT) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4, and 3/4 of 4 outcomes is 3.

widget.prompt: Flip two coins. How many of the 4 outcomes show at least one head?

commonErrors.feedback: That is HH only. HT and TH each contain a head too, so they also count as "at least one".
That is "exactly one head" (HT and TH). HH has two heads, which is still at least one.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only TT has zero heads, so the other three outcomes — HH, HT, TH — all qualify.
